title: Show HN: Sibyl – self-hosted cross-agent memory for AI coding agents
author: hyperb1iss
raw_text: I realized last year that I needed a better shared substrate for all the parallel coding (and other) agents I run if I wanted all my ADHD agentically-engineered dreams to come true. It started off as a simple Kanban board for agents with a crawler and rag, but it's long since evolved into a high performance, scalable, multi-user, self-hostable agent memory system built on SurrealDB that I can't live without. It's the thing that's helped me go absurdly parallel without just turning into a slop cannon.If an agent can use a CLI (or MCP, but CLI works better) it can speak Sibyl. You can run it locally, on a VPS in Docker, on Kubernetes, or wherever. The benchmarks and evals are competitive (96.96% strict recall@5 on LongMemEval-S, on the live API path, with no LLM in the retrieval path), and are actively expanding.My Sibyl knows everything about all of my projects, and it's ingested all my notes, docs, and even email. I can start an agent anywhere and it immediately knows where to go next. And it's all stored on my own infra.I just tagged 1.0.2 and use it every day. It's Apache 2.0 licensed and totally open source, contributions are welcome. Check it out and tell me if it works for you as well as it does for me!https://github.com/hyperb1iss/sibyl
summary: sibyl is a self-hosted, high-performance memory system designed for ai coding agents. it allows multiple agents to share information and collaborate effectively, moving beyond isolated operations. initially a kanban board with retrieval-augmented generation (rag) capabilities, it has grown into a scalable, multi-user system built on surrealdb. this matters significantly for you as you delve into ai agents and genai. when you're orchestrating complex agent systems, especially for tasks like coding or r&d, enabling agents to have shared context and learn from each other is a fundamental challenge. sibyl offers a practical solution to this, allowing for more parallel and sophisticated agentic workflows. you could try thinking about how you would implement shared memory in your own multi-agent projects, using sibyl as an architectural inspiration.
why: Enables complex, collaborative multi-agent systems with shared, persistent memory for better performance.

title: Towards Automating Scientific Review with Google's Paper Assistant Tool
author: Rajesh Jayaram, Drew Tyler, David Woodruff, Corinna Cortes, Yossi Matias, Vahab Mirrokni, Vincent Cohen-Addad
raw_text:
Artificial intelligence is driving a revolution in scientific discovery, accelerating everything from hypothesis generation to mathematical theorem proving. However, this rapid acceleration is creating a systemic challenge: traditional human peer review cannot scale to match the influx of AI-assisted science. Ultimately, to resolve this tension, we must also deploy AI to accelerate the verification and review process itself. To frame the discussion around this transition, we propose a taxonomy consisting of four progressive levels of AI-human collaboration in scientific evaluation, and discuss various trade-offs involved with each.
  As a step toward this future, we introduce the Paper Assistant Tool (PAT), an agentic AI framework built for deep scientific review and verification. PAT ingests full scientific manuscripts and produces a comprehensive evaluation, checking theoretical results, validating experiments, suggesting improvements, and identifying potential flaws. By utilizing inference scaling techniques, PAT is able to identify deeper issues than a single model call alone, achieving a 34% improvement over zero-shot recall on mathematical errors in the SPOT benchmark. Pilot deployments of PAT as a pre-submission tool for authors at two major Computer Science conferences -- STOC and ICML -- demonstrate its ability to identify critical errors and suggest substantive improvements to research papers. By catching errors early, PAT eases the cognitive burden placed on referees, while preserving their control over the outcomes of the review process.
summary: This paper discusses using artificial intelligence, specifically google's paper assistant tool, to automate parts of the scientific review process. The core idea is that as ai accelerates scientific discovery, the traditional human peer review system struggles to keep up. Therefore, ai itself needs to step in to help verify and review new research. For you, this is a compelling application of ai, potentially leveraging llms and agent-like systems, to solve a real-world scaling challenge in academia. Understanding how ai can process, evaluate, and summarize complex information is valuable for building advanced genai applications and agents. You could try considering how an llm, possibly augmented with rag, could be fine-tuned to perform specific review tasks like identifying key findings or checking for consistency.
why: Illustrates AI, LLMs, and agents automating complex, knowledge-intensive tasks like review.

title: Dialogue to Detection: A Multimodal Hybrid NLP Pipeline for Insurance Fraud Detection
author: Muhammad Shakeel Akram, Amal Htait, Abdul Hamid Sadka, Emma Meisingseth, Karishma Jaitly
raw_text: Insurance fraud imposes substantial financial losses and operational inefficiencies, raising premiums and impacting trust among legitimate policyholders. Early detection at FNOL remains a persistent challenge. Existing approaches rely largely on private, text-only datasets, limiting progress on multimodal methods that integrate linguistic, behavioural, and speaker-based indicators. We introduce a synthetic multimodal framework that replicates FNOL conditions. It generates agent-customer dialogue transcripts and two-speaker audios, performs ASR and diarisation. Downstream modules combine NER, regex-based feature extraction, LLM-RAG retrieval, and speaker embeddings in a rule-based risk score to flag narrative reuse, structural inconsistencies, and cross-case voice repetition while balancing sensitivity and false positives. Dataset validation and component-level evaluations show stability and transfer potential, offering a reproducible baseline beyond text-only fraud detection.
summary: This paper introduces a multimodal NLP pipeline designed to detect insurance fraud early, specifically during the first notice of loss (FNOL) conversations between agents and customers. It highlights that current methods often rely only on text, missing out on crucial linguistic, behavioral, and speaker-based cues. The researchers propose a synthetic data framework to generate realistic multimodal dialogues, which is a clever way to overcome the challenge of limited real-world data. For you, this is highly relevant as it combines natural language processing with other data types (multimodal AI) and addresses a significant real-world problem with financial implications. You could explore how different data modalities (text, audio features, sentiment) can be integrated in an AI pipeline for better performance, and consider the role of synthetic data in overcoming data scarcity.
why: Applies multimodal NLP to detect real-world fraud, using synthetic data generation.

title: 🚀 Why ChatGPT Hallucinates (And How RAG Fixes It) #RAG #LLM #GenerativeAI
author: Bit Yodha
summary: this resource explains a critical challenge with large language models (llms) called 'hallucinations,' where they generate factually incorrect or nonsensical information, and how retrieval-augmented generation (rag) offers a solution. llms, by their nature, are trained on vast amounts of data and can sometimes generate plausible-sounding but false statements. rag addresses this by first retrieving relevant, verified information from an external knowledge base (like a database or documents) and then feeding that information to the llm. this process 'grounds' the llm's response in factual data, significantly reducing the likelihood of hallucinations and making the output more reliable and trustworthy. understanding this is fundamental for building dependable generative ai applications. always consider how to integrate external knowledge to ensure factual accuracy in your llm projects.
why: explains a core llm problem (hallucinations) and rag's practical solution.

title: content in OpenAI ChatCompletion messages is a list, not string (lastmile-ai/mcp-agent)
raw_text:
content in OpenAI ChatCompletion messages is a list, not string — open-source issue in lastmile-ai/mcp-agent. Labels: bug, good first issue. use home assistant as mcp server,  then Calling OpenAI ChatCompletion with messages,  but the content in message is a list structure.

OpenAI API Specification：
- content can only be a string or null.
- It cannot be a list, object, or any other type.

If content is a list,  some LLM(deepseek) return the following error:
`[mcp_agent.workflows.llm.augmented_llm_openai] Error: Failed to deserialize the JSON body into the target type: messages[2]: invalid type: sequence, expected a string at line 1
summary: This is an open-source bug report highlighting a common issue where the `content` field in OpenAI's `ChatCompletion` API messages is sometimes incorrectly passed as a list instead of a string or null, as specified by the API. This can cause errors, especially with other LLMs that strictly follow the API specification. As an AI/Data Science student, you'll frequently interact with APIs, especially for LLMs. Understanding API specifications and common pitfalls, like data type mismatches, is vital for debugging and building robust applications.
